title: MRMhub-viz: Integration Visualizer
text: MRMhub-viz is a standalone, interactive application for reviewing the peak-integration results produced by INTEGRATOR (see Running INTEGRATOR — Step 3). It is distributed as a self-contained executable (~10 MB), resides in the same folder as the MRMhub application, and is launched like any other application. Because it reads the binary results written to the misc/ folder during peak integration, Step 3 must have been run at least once before the visualizer can display a dataset.

title: MRMhub-viz: Integration Visualizer
text:
What it displays
The transition to be inspected is selected from the dropdown menu in the top-left corner. For the selected transition, the extracted ion chromatograms of the individual samples are shown together with the detected peak and its left and right integration borders, so that the integration can be reviewed across the entire analytical sequence at a glance. Moving the pointer over a chromatogram reports the exact retention time at the cursor — the value used when defining fixed peak borders in the transition list (see Input Files — Transition list).

title: MRMhub-viz: Integration Visualizer
text:
The review → refine loop
MRMhub-viz is the inspection half of an iterative loop between visual review and parameter adjustment. Automated integration is rarely optimal for every feature on the first pass; the visualizer identifies where it fails, and the input files are adjusted to correct it. A typical cycle proceeds as follows.

Inspect. Step through the transitions and confirm that the intended peak is detected and correctly bounded, both in the reference samples and across the sequence. Look for missed peaks, co-integrated neighbours, truncated tails, and failures of retention-time tracking.
Diagnose. Relate each problem to the setting responsible for it — a missed peak to RT_tol or RT_shift, a co-integrated neighbour to peak_width, an untracked retention-time jump to RT_shift_bound (see Effects of the key settings).
Refine. Adjust the global parameters in param.txt, or add per-feature overrides in the transition list (peak width, uniform_width, fixed integration bounds) for the problematic minority. Individual peaks that resist automated integration can also have their borders edited directly in RT_matrix.csv.
Re-integrate. After a change to param.txt or the transition list, re-run peak finding (Steps 1–2) followed by integration (Step 3); when only RT_matrix.csv has been edited, re-run Step 3 alone. Reload the dataset in MRMhub-viz and repeat until the integration is satisfactory.







Tip



Refine globally first, then per-feature. Tune param.txt so that the majority of peaks integrate correctly, and reserve transition-list overrides and fixed borders for the remaining difficult peaks. Confirm every change in MRMhub-viz before re-integrating the whole dataset — see the peak-width recommendations.








Warning



Re-running Step 2 overwrites RT_matrix.csv. Any manual edits to the integration borders are lost when peak finding is re-run. Make manual RT_matrix.csv adjustments only once the automated integration is otherwise final, then run Step 3 (see Running INTEGRATOR — Step 2).

Running INTEGRATOR — re-run peak finding and integration after each change.
Sharing Results — bundle the visualizer with the dataset for review by others.

title: Download & Project Setup
text:
Important



INTEGRATOR is not installed. It is a self-contained, portable executable: there is no installer, and nothing is added to the system. It is downloaded, unzipped, and run from a folder.

title: Download & Project Setup
text:
One copy per project
The recommended approach is to keep one copy of the INTEGRATOR folder inside each data-analysis project, alongside that project’s raw data and input files. Because the executable, the parameters (param.txt), the input files, and the results reside together in one self-contained folder, the entire analysis remains reproducible: the folder can be re-opened months later, a parameter adjusted, and the integration re-run exactly as before. Different projects can also use different versions of INTEGRATOR without interfering with each other.






Note



INTEGRATOR is not required to use the QUANT R package; QUANT imports directly from vendor outputs (MassHunter, Skyline) as well. See the QUANT documentation ↗.

title: Download & Project Setup
text:
Get the application
INTEGRATOR is distributed as pre-compiled executables for Windows and macOS, available from https://github.com/SLINGhub/MRMhub/releases. Unzip the downloaded file and copy the folder into the project location. The folder comprises the following files and subfolders: MRMhub is the main application, and MRMhub-viz is an application for reviewing peak integration results.

title: Download & Project Setup
text:
First launch (clear the security prompt)
The executable is unsigned, so the operating system displays a one-time security warning on first launch. Clear it as follows.
On macOS, the following error is shown:





To resolve this, go to “Systems Settings”, “Privacy & Security” tab, and click “Open Anyway” button to enable the software.





On Windows, right-click on the executable, select “Properties”, and on the “General” tab, check the “Unblock” box near the bottom if available, then click OK or Apply.

title: Download & Project Setup
text:
Folder layout
The input files required by the MRMhub application are feature_list.csv, run_order.csv, and param.txt. The mzML folder is used to store the mzML data files. All of these are explained in Input Files. Furthermore, this distribution contains a test dataset, with a complete set of input and raw data files, which can be used as templates for future analysis. The MRMhub_plot.r is an R script used to generate the PDFs. It can be modified to tailor for specific layouts and design features of the plots.

title: Input Files
text: INTEGRATOR reads three input files together with the mzML/ data folder. This page documents each of them. For how the software uses these settings internally, see the Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm.

title: Input Files
text:
Global parameters (param.txt)
The software requires a global parameter file (param.txt by default), which directs it to the required information and controls peak detection and integration.








Parameter
Description
Default




mzML_files
Location of the mzML files used for peak integration.
mzML


batch_info
Input file listing the mzML file names and their metadata (see below).
run_order.csv


transition_list
Input file with the MRM transition information (see below).
feature_list.csv


peak_width
[w, x, y, z] define the allowed integration bounds: the left border falls w–x min and the right border y–z min from the apex (see below).
[0.17, 0.05, 0.1, 0.35]


num_threads
Number of CPU threads used for the integration task.
2


mz_tol
Tolerance between the indicated and the detected m/z values.
0.06


RT_tol
Tolerance between the indicated and the detected RT. A key setting when processing complex chromatograms.
0.1


RT_shift
[x, y] bound the RT drift relative to the reference samples: the peak may lie at most x min earlier and y min later than expected. The lower bound is written as a negative value (earlier RT); the upper bound is positive (later RT). Setting [0, 0] disables RT-shift correction.
[-0.2, 0.2]


RT_shift_bound
Maximum allowed RT drift between adjacent samples.
0.1









Tip



Worked example. A published lipidomics dataset (Agilent triple-quadrupole) used mz_tol = 0.06, RT_tol = 0.04, and peak_width = [0.15, 0.08, 0.08, 0.18] globally, with per-feature overrides for broad or convoluted peaks, an RT-shift window of (-0.1, 0.4), and a maximum sample-to-sample RT shift (RT_shift_bound) of 0.05. These values provide reasonable starting points for a fast, well-resolved method. See the full Dataset 3 workflow ↗ for the complete input files and the resulting integration.





The param.txt file used for the Dataset 3 worked example, showing all configured parameters and their values.

title: Input Files
text:
Sample list (run_order.csv)
This file lists the data files to be processed. The file names must be given in their processing order, from top to bottom. mzML files present in the data folder but not listed here are ignored. Columns containing required information for individual data files are marked in bold.



Column
Description




file name
The mzML file names to be processed, located in the folder defined under mzML_files in param.txt. Must include the .mzML extension.


batch
The analysis batch identifier the file belongs to. This value has no function inside INTEGRATOR, but is carried through to the result.


sample_type
The sample (QC) type of the corresponding sample. Blanks must be labelled with text containing BLK, as these are processed differently (see below). For all other cases, any sample type may be defined, and the information is forwarded to the integration results; the field may also be left empty. Use of the default MRMhub QC types (see QUANT — Sample Types & QC Roles) is recommended to ensure reliable integration with the QUANT module.


reference
Indicates that the sample is used as a reference for RT-shift estimation (see below). Label with x. When selecting multiple samples, ensure they exhibit negligible RT shifts relative to one another.









Note



How sample_type is used. INTEGRATOR distinguishes only blanks (any sample_type containing the text BLK), which are processed differently during peak finding, from non-blanks. Every other sample/QC-type label has no effect inside INTEGRATOR; it is carried through to long.csv for use by the QUANT module. Using the standard MRMhub QC nomenclature here allows QUANT to assign the QC roles automatically.





A portion of the sample list from the Dataset 3 worked example. The first two BQC samples, located early in the analytical sequence, were designated as retention-time reference anchors (the reference column).

title: Input Files
text:
Transition / Feature list (feature_list.csv)
This file specifies the transitions to be processed and the features to be integrated for each transition. Transitions present in the mzML files but not listed here are ignored. Columns containing required information for each feature are marked in bold.







Column
Description




Compound Name
Feature (analyte) identifier. Must be a unique value, typically identifying a single peak. Multiple distinct features can be defined for one transition.


Transition Name
Transition identifier. Values may be repeated.


ISTD
The internal standard feature assigned to the corresponding compound. This value currently has no function in the INTEGRATOR modules, but is included in the results and read by the QUANT module. May be left empty; if defined, it must correspond to a defined Compound Name.


Precursor Ion
The m/z value of the precursor ion. Must match the corresponding value in the mzML file within the tolerance set by mz_tol in param.txt.


Product Ion
The m/z value of the product ion. Must match the corresponding value in the mzML file within the tolerance set by mz_tol in param.txt.


RT
The expected retention time of the corresponding feature, in minutes.


uniform_width
Either y or n (default). If y, the peak boundaries are set to the median of the automatically determined borders.


left integration bound
Sets a fixed left peak border for all samples, in minutes (with respect to the reference sample).


right integration bound
Sets a fixed right peak border for all samples, in minutes (with respect to the reference sample).


peak width
[w, x, y, z] define the allowed integration bounds: left = w–x min, right = y–z min from the apex (see below). Overrides the globally defined peak_width in param.txt.


Remarks
Used to document integration settings.

title: Input Files
text:
Effects of the key settings
Most settings trade sensitivity (finding and fully capturing the intended peak) against specificity (not grabbing a neighbouring transition, an adjacent peak, or noise). The table below summarises what happens at each extreme; the peak-width recommendations below provide further detail on peak_width, the most influential setting for difficult chromatograms. For the algorithm that consumes these settings, see the Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm.









Setting
What it controls
Too small/narrow
Too large/wide




mz_tol
How far the detected m/z may deviate from the value in the transition list
A transition may not be matched at all if the instrument’s m/z calibration is slightly off
A nearby transition / channel may be matched by mistake


RT_tol
The retention-time window searched around the expected RT (key for complex chromatograms)
The peak is missed when its RT drifts beyond the window
A wrong, co-eluting, or adjacent peak may be selected instead of the intended one


peak_width [w,x,y,z]
Allowed windows for the left (w–x) and right (y–z) peak borders, relative to the apex
Incomplete integration — tailing or broadened peaks get cut short
Smaller adjacent/interfering peaks get co-integrated into the area


RT_shift [x,y]
The maximum RT drift expected across the reference samples
Genuine drift between references is not accommodated, hurting peak tracking
The algorithm searches an unnecessarily wide window, raising the chance of picking the wrong peak


RT_shift_bound
The maximum RT drift allowed between adjacent samples
A real run-to-run RT jump can break sample-to-sample tracking
Spurious jumps may be followed, tracking drift that isn’t there


num_threads
CPU threads used for integration
Slower processing only — no effect on results
Faster, bounded by available cores — no effect on results









Tip



Adjust globally in param.txt to suit the majority of peaks, then use per-feature overrides in the transition list (peak width, uniform_width, fixed integration bounds) only for the problematic minority. Always confirm the effect of a change visually in MRMhub-viz before re-integrating the whole dataset.

title: Input Files
section: Recommendations for setting peak integration parameters
text:
Recommendations for setting peak integration parameters
The peak_width parameter, defined globally in param.txt and optionally per feature in the Transition List, is a key setting for automated integration of complex chromatograms. Values are specified in the format [w, x, y, z], where the ranges w–x and y–z define the allowed windows for the left and right peak borders, respectively. The integration algorithm is constrained to set peak start and end points within these ranges, even if its automatic boundary detection would otherwise extend beyond them.
Ranges that are too narrow may lead to incomplete integration, particularly for tailing peaks or peaks of unstable width, whereas ranges that are too wide may cause smaller adjacent peaks to be included in the integration. A global setting that suits the majority of peaks in the dataset should be defined in param.txt, with per-feature settings applied to convoluted, asymmetric, or otherwise broadened peaks. Narrower per-feature ranges can also be used where nearby interferences are not recognised as separate peaks and are consequently co-integrated.








Examples of manually set peak boundaries in INTEGRATOR. (a, b) Effect of the peak_width parameter on a peak with clear tailing (PC 36:6): (a) the global setting, suitable for the majority of peaks, and (b) a feature-specific peak width overriding the global value for improved integration. (c, d) Effect on a peak with nearby interferences (PC O-38:4): (c) the global setting, and (d) an excessively wide peak_width that causes incorrect integration, underscoring the importance of an appropriate global value. (e, f) A complex chromatogram of three overlapping LPC 17:0 isomers: (e) the global setting yields only partial integration, with the first peak unrecognised, whereas (f) fixed boundaries defined for the first peak enable correct picking and integration of all three isomers.


Set the uniform_width parameter to true for features whose integration is correct in most samples but incorrect or inaccurate in a minority.
Use fixed left/right integration bound times where automated integration, even after tuning the peak_width settings, does not correctly and consistently integrate convoluted peaks or peaks with nearby interferences. These hard border settings are recommended only as a last resort, since fixed borders may require re-adjustment when the same analytical method is applied to other datasets. Note: These defined borders are still adjusted for retention-time shifts.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text: This page is a reference for the algorithm that detects, picks, and integrates MRM peaks inside INTEGRATOR. It describes what the software does internally; for the operational menu steps see Running INTEGRATOR, and for how to set each parameter mentioned below see Input Files.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Implementation
INTEGRATOR and its viewer app are implemented as a self-contained, light-weight application for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows 11 (x64) that requires no installation. It provides a terminal user interface, while its viewer (MRMhub-viz) comes with a graphical interface.
Considering the scalability to large-scale projects (e.g. > 10,000 samples), INTEGRATOR avoids loading the data from all mzML files into memory simultaneously. Instead, it first surveys peak features across all samples and writes the information to the file system as binary files, which are reloaded as needed in subsequent steps. This design significantly reduces the memory footprint and processing time for large-scale datasets, making it executable on relatively modest hardware — such as a standard laptop.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Sample and transition-list validation
The mzML file names in the sample-list file are checked against the actual files in the data directory provided by the user. Files absent from the directory are reported in a text file (missing_files.txt) so the user can check them. The input transition list is used to assign transition names and attributes to the chromatograms in each mzML file by matching precursor-ion m/z, product-ion m/z, and RT. Transitions that fail to match any chromatogram are skipped and reported in a text file (missing_compounds.txt). Chromatograms in mzML files without any assignment are also excluded from the analysis. The user may proceed with the analysis even if some files or compounds are missing.
Where the same transition (same Q1/Q3 values) with identical or nearly identical MRM start and end windows appears two or more times in an mzML file, the user is alerted and can choose which transition/MRM index to map to which feature in the transition input file.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Retention-time shift correction
The algorithm begins with an initial RT-drift estimation. For each transition, it treats the ion trace in the user-designated reference sample(s) as the reference pattern and uses it to track potential RT drift in all samples. The reference samples are expected to be selected from an early part of the analysis sequence, and not dispersed throughout the entire sequence. The chromatograms in all samples are then aligned to those of the reference samples within individual MRM windows, yielding estimates of the RT shifts.
The user can set a maximum allowance of RT drift (in minutes) in the parameter file (param.txt) using the RT_shift parameter. The syntax is RT_shift = [x, y], where x and y are the forward and backward drift allowances: the algorithm interprets that the RT drift is no more than x minutes earlier and no more than y minutes later than the expected RT in the reference samples. In addition, the RT_shift_bound parameter restricts the RT shift between adjacent sample injections.
RT-shift correction can be disabled by setting RT_shift = [0, 0], which can help for datasets with strong variability of features and/or interferences in the chromatograms, where the cross-correlation approach may yield inaccurate results. In the absence of chromatographic peaks for blank samples, their RT shifts are determined by interpolation from the shifts observed in adjacent samples of the analytical sequence.
When the user chooses to process only a specific part of the chromatograms — by globally setting an RT window relative to the expected RT — RT-shift correction is performed only on the corresponding RT window.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Feature detection
INTEGRATOR performs a first-round search of peak features in all files using continuous wavelet transform (CWT)–based pattern matching. For each MRM window, using the resulting survey of features, the algorithm determines the target number of features per transition as the median number of features detected in the initial survey, and treats it as the upper limit for the number of stable, consistent features to report in the second-round survey.
In the second round, the algorithm maps all peak features across the samples, connecting each peak in one sample to the corresponding peak in the next sample so that every reported feature is stable (i.e. can be detected as a feature) and consistent. The key part of this mapping is that peaks are matched while accounting for the RT drift estimated above. The user sets the RT_tol parameter to indicate the maximum deviation of RT from the value given in the method table. If no feature can be detected within this bound, the integrated area is reported as zero.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Determination of peak integration borders
In the final step, the algorithm goes through the transitions to finalize the integration borders.
For the simple case of unimodal ion traces, the user can set the peak_width parameter quartet [w, x, y, z] to define the default start and end integration points. This can be customized for individual analytes with a peak width column in the transition-list table. The user can also set the uniform_width option (its own column in the transition table) so that the integration width remains the same between samples for a given transition, and can set fixed left/right integration bounds to fix the integration points with respect to the reference samples.
In complex cases — ion traces showing multiple peaks with or without baseline separation — the algorithm searches for valleys between features to cut the integration in the drift-corrected RT space, reconverts the border positions to the original RT space, and writes all RT borders to a CSV file (RT_matrix.csv) for user inspection and optional manual adjustment before peak areas are calculated.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Baseline determination
The baseline is determined on the x axis from the integration borders. On the y axis, three modes are available:

5th percentile (default) — a horizontal baseline set at the 5th percentile of the intensities within the integration window.
v_drop — a horizontal baseline set at the minimum of the left and right border y values of the curve.
Valley-to-valley — a sloped baseline fitted between the points where the left and right integration borders intersect the ion trace.







Note



Where to set these parameters. RT_shift, RT_shift_bound, RT_tol, peak_width, uniform_width, and the fixed integration bounds are all configured in param.txt and the transition list — see Input Files for the syntax, defaults, and tuning recommendations. To see the algorithm in action across the four processing steps, see Running INTEGRATOR.

title: INTEGRATOR
text:
INTEGRATOR is the stand-alone peak-integration module of the MRMhub pipeline. It reads converted mzML files, detects and integrates MRM peaks across all samples, supports interactive review and refinement of the results, and exports tables for quantitation.
It is distributed as a self-contained executable for macOS and Windows and requires no installation and no separate runtime. Retaining one copy in each analysis project folder keeps the project reproducible.

title: MSConvert Instructions
text:
Next

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
flow chart for MRMhub INTEGRATOR
Upon execution, the software launches a terminal user interface with four menu options. For new datasets, steps 1 and 2 are applied sequentially. The final step 4 is optional and used only when integration results as PDF files are required.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
Step 1 — Data Validation
The first step verifies the files and information provided in the input files. Inconsistencies are reported in text files saved to the same directory as the MRMhub application. These files are generated only when issues are identified.

missing_files.txt lists mzML files that are present in the data folder but not listed in the Sample List, as well as files listed in the Sample List but absent from the data folder.
missing_compounds.txt reports transitions defined in the Transition List but not found in all mzML files. Note: Transitions present only in a subset of the mzML files are currently not processed.
missing_details.txt details the missing transitions and identifies exactly which samples lack them. This is useful when a transition appears in some samples but not others.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
section: Step 2 — Peak Finding and RT-shift estimation
text:
Step 2 — Peak Finding and RT-shift estimation
The second step runs the peak finding and picking algorithm (see Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm for how it works). The result of this step is a table of identified peaks (features) with their left and right peak borders in each sample. This table is saved as the CSV file RT_matrix.csv in the same folder as the application and is required for step 3.
These integration bounds may be refined further on a per-transition and per-sample basis before peak integration is performed in step 3. For a new dataset, the recommended approach is to proceed directly to peak integration, followed by visualization of the results in steps 3 (and 4), and to adjust specific integration borders manually only afterward. Manual adjustment is generally discouraged unless certain integrations can only be achieved through it.
At this point, the integration visualizer application MRMhub-viz (see MRMhub-viz Visualizer) can be launched to inspect the integration results. Global and per-feature integration parameters can then be revised (via param.txt and the Transition List), and peak integration re-attempted via steps 1 and 2.
Once automated integration is considered optimal, final manual adjustments to individual peaks can be made in RT_matrix.csv (see Step 2). After these optional manual adjustments, the final peak integration is performed by (re-)running step 3.
Warning: Each time step 2 is executed, RT_matrix.csv is overwritten and any manual modifications are lost.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
Step 3 — Peak Integration
In the third step, the peaks identified in step 2 are integrated and the corresponding results saved to the following default output files:

quant_raw.csv A wide-format table of peak areas. The top three rows additionally contain the precursor and product m/z and peak apex retention time values.
long.csv A long-format table containing peak area, height, peak apex retention time, FWHM (Full Width at Half Maximum) and integration borders. The corresponding precursor and product m/z values, the analysis time stamp (extracted from the mzML files) and the metadata from the input files (sample type, ISTD, batch identifier) are also included.
misc A folder containing the peak integration results in a binary format, used by the visualizer application MRMhub-viz and in step 4.

All output tables are plain comma-separated CSV files. long.csv is the canonical hand-off to QUANT (one row per sample × feature); quant_raw.csv is a wide-format export of peak areas and is not read by the QUANT module.






Notelong.csv columns





These are the columns QUANT’s import_data_mrmhub() reads from long.csv. Only feature_name and raw_data_filename are strictly required (plus at least one intensity column); the rest are metadata and measurements carried through to the MRMhubExperiment.







long.csv column
Meaning




raw_data_filename
Source mzML file name (becomes the analysis identifier)


time_stamp
Acquisition timestamp, read from the mzML


sample_type
Sample / QC type, from run_order.csv


batch
Batch identifier, from run_order.csv


feature_name
Feature (analyte) identifier, from the transition list


internal_standard
Assigned ISTD feature, from the transition list


rt_apex
Retention time at the peak apex (min)


area
Integrated peak area


height
Peak height


FWHM
Full width at half maximum


rt_int_start / rt_int_end
Left / right integration borders (min)


polarity
Ionisation polarity


precursor_mz / product_mz
Transition m/z values


collision_energy
Collision energy



quant_raw.csv is a wide table of peak areas (features × samples); its top rows additionally carry the precursor and product m/z and the apex retention time per transition.









Tip



Continue post-processing in QUANT. The long.csv file is the canonical hand-off into the QUANT R package: import_data_mrmhub(path = "path/to/long.csv", import_metadata = TRUE) loads the file and its embedded metadata into an MRMhubExperiment for ISTD normalisation, drift/batch correction, QC, and reporting. See the QUANT documentation ↗.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
Step 4 — Generate PDF results (optional)
The fourth step, which is optional, produces integration results as PDF files. It creates three folders with different types of results:

by_transition: Contains one PDF per transition, with chromatograms plotted for each sample. Only transitions with at least one feature (peak) exceeding the minimum intensity threshold value are included here (see by_transition_low).
by_transition_low: Contains PDFs of transitions where none of the integrated features (peaks) had an area exceeding the minimum intensity threshold defined by the constant low_intensity_threshold in the provided MRMhub_plot.r R script.
by_sample: Provides a PDF for each reference sample; all of the sample’s transitions are plotted within the same file.

For efficient viewing of PDFs on macOS, open the PDF folder, press Space to start Quick Look, then use the up/down arrow keys to move between transitions (files). Use the scroll wheel or trackpad to scroll through each PDF.
Note: In large-scale projects, generating many large PDF files can take considerable time, depending on computer performance and the number of cores used. The number of cores used to generate the PDFs can be adjusted via the constant ncores in the provided MRMhub_plot.r script.






Note



Reviewing retention-time stability at scale. The per-transition PDFs provide an efficient means of confirming that RT-shift correction has tracked the peaks across the entire analytical sequence. In a published 4,591-sample lipidomics analysis, for example, RT shifts remained below 0.04 min across the whole run, with the exception of approximately 20 samples at the start of one batch near the end of the sequence, which were readily identified by scanning the by_transition PDFs. See the Dataset 3 workflow ↗.

title: Sharing Results & Reproducible Workflows
text: Because INTEGRATOR and MRMhub-viz are self-contained executables that require no installation, a complete peak-integration dataset can be shared as a single folder, allowing others to inspect, reproduce, and modify the raw-data processing. Beyond the CSV tables of peak areas, the raw data, the input files with all integration parameters, and the individual integration results can be bundled together with the applications.

title: Sharing Results & Reproducible Workflows
text:
What to bundle
The components below make a shared dataset fully self-contained. The raw data and input files are what is needed to re-run the processing; the results allow the outcome to be inspected without re-running; and the applications provide the means to do either.

Raw data and input files







Item
Purpose




mzML/ folder
The converted raw data on which integration is performed.


param.txt
All global parameters (tolerances, peak-width windows, RT-shift bounds, threads).


run_order.csv
The sample list, in processing order, with sample/QC types and reference-sample designations.


feature_list.csv
The transitions and features to integrate, including any per-feature overrides.





Results



Item
Purpose




long.csv
The canonical long-format results and the hand-off to the QUANT R package.


quant_raw.csv
The wide-format table of peak areas.


RT_matrix.csv
The finalised integration borders, including any manual adjustments — required to reproduce the exact integration.


misc/ folder
The binary integration results read by MRMhub-viz for interactive review.


PDF folders (optional)
by_transition, by_transition_low, and by_sample PDFs documenting the integration (see Running INTEGRATOR — Step 4).





Applications



Item
Purpose




MRMhub (~1 MB)
The integration application, to re-run or modify any processing step.


MRMhub-viz (~10 MB)
The visualizer, to review the integration interactively (see MRMhub-viz).


MRMhub_plot.r
The base-R script that generates the PDF results; it can be edited to tailor the plot layout.









Tip



Retaining one copy of the applications in each analysis project folder keeps the project reproducible and self-documenting: a recipient can open MRMhub-viz to inspect every peak, or re-run INTEGRATOR to reproduce or adjust the integration, without any installation.
